new_statements.relation_note: Partly agrees, partly contradicts the catalog's fixed: final syllable line: final stress holds only for Atayal-origin words; Japanese-origin words (about 65% of basic vocabulary per Sanada & Chien) are penultimate when three or more syllables and weight-sensitive when disyllabic. Dialect-specific (Aohua). Same author and topic as the unobtained 2022 MA thesis (index 1).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Aohua dialect, one female consultant in her 50s. Stress placement depends on the word's origin and its syllable count: Atayal-origin words of any length take final stress (papak 'ear', lukus 'clothes', tahi 'ant', kuleh 'fish', stress on the last syllable); Japanese-origin monosyllables are stressed trivially; Japanese-origin words of three or more syllables take penultimate stress (karara 'body', kuruma 'car', zidensya 'bicycle', kucibiru 'lips'); Japanese-origin disyllables are weight-sensitive, stress going to the heavier syllable by the hierarchy VV > Vn > VG > V (seenen, kanzyoo, nansay, suyren, kaban, opay); with equal weight either syllable may be stressed or the placement is lexical (neko, yuki, ningen).
new_statements.exceptions: Equal-weight Japanese-origin disyllables: free variation (hari~hari, umi~umi, mizyu~mizyu) or lexically fixed (neko, kusa, ningen); no words of five or more syllables found. Section 4.4 (p. 59) summarises other dialects: Tongyueh per Sanada (2013) final or penultimate (Atayal final vs Seediq penultimate), without examples; Hanhsi per Qiu (2015: 39) normally final.
new_statements.identity_note: Yilan Creole is spoken in four villages (Tongyueh, Hanhsi, Chinyang, Aohua), each with a distinct dialect (Sanada & Chien 2008, cited in Lin 2021 p. 55). Sanada & Chien 2012's final-accent statement rests on Tongyueh data; Qiu 2015's final-stress statement is treated by Lin 2021 (p. 59) as Hanhsi; Lin 2021 (and the unobtained Lin 2022 thesis) describe the Aohua dialect from a single female consultant in her 50s; Sanada 2013 notes speaker-internal variation and a possible Seediq contribution to the penultimate variant. The catalog name is Vernacular Atayalic Japanese (Tan 2023's term); the older literature calls it Yilan Creole / 宜蘭クレオール.

new_statements.translation: Accent is non-distinctive and is placed on the final syllable or on the second syllable from the end. However, there is no phonological opposition between the two. [...] In Yilan Creole, however, a tendency is noted for the position of the accent to fluctuate, between individuals and within one individual, word by word, between the final and the penultimate syllable. [...] That is, I suspect that the placement of the accent on the penultimate syllable is a faint vestige of Seediq.

new_statements.quote: In terms of suprasegmental features, according to Qiu (2015: 39), stress in Vernacular Atayalic Japanese always falls on the final syllable of the word regardless of the word's origin, as illustrated by Japanese-derived [waha] '1sg' and Atayal-derived [lalaŋ] 'before'. If this is the case, it is reasonable to conclude that the prosody of Vernacular Atayalic Japanese mirrors the Atayal system of word-final syllable stress. By contrast, Japanese is a pitch accent language with various accent patterns. However, my data show that in Vernacular Atayalic Japanese words in isolation can have non-word-final stress patterns. Due to limited space, I will discuss this issue in a separate paper.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog codes yila1234 as fixed final stress (final stress, our earlier survey-2026-08-31). Lin 2022 agrees with final stress only for the Atayal-origin stratum of the Aohua dialect; for Japanese-origin words (most of the lexicon) it describes a different TYPE: weight-sensitive stress in a final two-syllable window (Vn > VG > VO > V), with penultimate default in words of three or more syllables and lexical placement in light CV.CV disyllables, plus phrase-level reassignment. That is a weight-sensitive/mixed system, not fixed final. Note the dialect split Lin himself reports (4.6): Hanhsi (Qiu 2015) = normally final, Tungyueh (Sanada 2013) = final or penultimate; the catalog's fixed: fin…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Aohua dialect of Yilan Creole (nouns and adjectives; verbs left for future work): stress placement depends on word origin, syllable weight and word length. (a) Atayal-origin words: fixed stress on the final syllable (he, abaw, lukus, tahi; monosyllables trivially stressed). (b) Japanese-origin words (the bulk of the lexicon): a two-syllable window at the right edge; stress goes to the heavier of the final two syllables by the four-way scale Vn > VG (vowel+/y/) > VO (obstruent coda) > V, onsets weightless (e.g. CVn.CV zenbu, onna -> initial; CV.CVn gohan, CV.CVG yasay, akay -> final; CV.CVn.CV zidensya -> penult; CV.CV.CVn nizikan -> final). Ties: in CV.CV disyllables placement is lexical/unpredictable and partly speaker-variable (kawa, tane, sita, buta on one syllable vs kori, saru, niku, hone on the other; ame, umi, tori vary), CVn.CVn disyllables are always final (ningen, genkin, hanbun); in words of three or more syllables with equal-weight final two syllables stress is penultimate (hirari, kuruma, kucibiru, butaniku, irootoko). (c) Phrase/clause level (4.4): one primary stress on the heavier of the last two syllables of the phonological phrase, penult on a tie, sentence-final particles (mo, ga) not counted. The thesis also states (p.11 fn.8) that Yilan Creole 'is a stress language and does not have a tone feature' (tones of Mandarin/Minnan loans are dropped), and (4.1-4.2) that stress is realised by pitch, duration and intensity, with duration and intensity given priority.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described at word level; the only primary/other distinction is at phrase level (4.4), where each word 'has its own stress when uttered separately' but the phonological phrase carries one primary stress within its last two syllables.
new_statements.exceptions: p.50-51: saygo 'last' (CVG.CV) and, for some speakers, sinzyo 'heart', kanzyo 'liver' (CVn.CV) stressed against the weight hierarchy -- 'the only exceptions I have in my data'; p.56 (106): tosiyori/tosyori 'elderly' has final rather than the expected penultimate stress; CV.CV disyllables are lexically unpredictable with inter-speaker variation (ame, umi, tori); no Atayal-origin words of 3+ syllables in the data; VG vs VO order rests on a single trisyllable (dayraksuy, p.55). p.61 §4.6: other dialects differ -- Tungyueh 'stress may appear on the last syllable or penultimate syllable' (after Sanada 2013, no examples given there), Hanhsi 'stress normally falls on the last syllable' (after Qiu 2015: waha, lalaN); Lin suggests these dialects may also turn out to have a weight-sensitive component.
new_statements.identity_note: Lin 2022 describes specifically the Aohua (澳花) village dialect of Yilan Creole (four consultants aged 58-72, fieldwork plus online sessions), and restricts the word-stress analysis to nouns and adjectives. The other three village dialects (Tungyueh, Hanhsi, Chinyang) are only summarised from Sanada 2013 and Qiu 2015 in section 4.6; the catalog's fixed: final syllable record corresponds to the Hanhsi description (Qiu 2015), not to Aohua.

readall_conflicts: The sources disagree by dialect and by lexical stratum. Sanada & Chien 2012 (p. 42, Tongyueh data) and Qiu 2015 (p. 39, Hanhsi per Lin) state non-contrastive final stress, inherited from Atayal, and Chien & Sanada 2011 (p. 77) reports the prosody as basically Atayal (citing the unobtained JPCL 2010 article). Sanada 2013 (p. 105) weakens this to final or penultimate, fluctuating by word and speaker with no phonological contrast, and suspects a Seediq (penultimate) substrate residue. Lin 2021 (pp. 54-57), for the Aohua dialect and one consultant, contradicts a blanket final rule: only Atayal-origin words are final; Japanese-origin words of three or more syllables are penultimate, and Japanese-origin disyllables are weight-sensitive (VV > Vn > VG > V, ties free or lexical). Tan 2023 (p. 337) likewise reports non-final stress in isolation forms in his own data without giving a rule. The catalog's fixed: final syllable line therefore matches the Tongyueh/Hanhsi descriptions and the Atayal-origin vocabulary everywhere, but not the Japanese-origin stratum of Aohua as described by Lin. One disagreement, and it runs along dialect lines. The catalog record (our earlier survey-2026-08-31) has Yilan Creole as fixed final stress. Lin 2022, the only full phonological description opened here, describes the Aohua dialect as a split system: Atayal-origin words take fixed final stress, but Japanese-origin words (the majority) take weight-sensitive stress on the heavier of the last two syllabl…

audit.recode_to: Not uniform 'fixed-dominant final'. reclassify as a non-contrastive, lexically/etymologically conditioned system: final stress on Atayal-stratum words; Japanese-stratum words (c. 65% of basic vocabulary per Sanada 2013) penultimate when 3+ syllables and weight-sensitive (VV>Vn>VG>V, else free/lexical) when disyllabic (Lin 2021, Aohua); Tungyueh described as final~penult fluctuating (Sanada 2013 p.105). If the catalog must keep a single fixed class, at minimum set not in the strict set, add a caution 'final vs penult varies by lexical stratum and village; weight-sensitive disyllables reported for Aohua', cite Lin 2021 pp.55-58 and Sanada 2013 p.105 alongside Qiu 2015 p.39, and fix the locator to p.39.
audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: Quote genuine (Qiu 2015 p.39, downloaded now; nothing was held before). But the deciding source is a syntax-focused MA thesis whose stress claim rests on two words from one village (Hanhsi) plus an appeal to Atayal. Every other first-hand source I opened either qualifies or contradicts uniform final stress: Sanada 2013 (Tungyueh) final or penult, fluctuating; Lin 2021 (Aohua, the only dedicated stress study) final only for the Atayal stratum, penult for Japanese-stratum polysyllables and weight-sensitive for Japanese disyllables; Tan 2023 reports non-final patterns in her own data. Only Sanada & Chien 2012 p.42 supports plain final. Since the Japanese stratum is the majority of the lexicon, 'final-dominant' is unlikely to survive a re-read; hence at-risk / reclassify.

If the two syllables have the same weight, stress falls on either syllable in an unpredictable way in the case of disyllabic words, or on penultimate in the case of longer words. [...] (85) Syllable weight hierarchy in Aohua: Vn > VG > VO > V"

sources.quote: Stress normally falls on the final syllable in Yilan Creole, as seen in [waha] 'I' (ED)(J) and [lalaŋ] 'before' (ED; A). This feature derives from Atayal, which is known to be a stress-final language (Li, 1980, p. 356).
